6:["$","div",null,{"className":"lg:col-span-8","children":[["$","header",null,{"className":"mb-12","children":[["$","h1",null,{"className":"font-serif font-light text-5xl md:text-6xl text-navy mb-4 leading-tight","children":"Tim Hector"}],["$","div",null,{"className":"w-24 h-[2px] bg-gold"}]]}],["$","section",null,{"className":"prose prose-navy max-w-none","children":[["$","div",null,{"className":"relative mb-12","children":[["$","$L3",null,{"iconNode":[["path",{"d":"M16 3a2 2 0 0 0-2 2v6a2 2 0 0 0 2 2 1 1 0 0 1 1 1v1a2 2 0 0 1-2 2 1 1 0 0 0-1 1v2a1 1 0 0 0 1 1 6 6 0 0 0 6-6V5a2 2 0 0 0-2-2z","key":"rib7q0"}],["path",{"d":"M5 3a2 2 0 0 0-2 2v6a2 2 0 0 0 2 2 1 1 0 0 1 1 1v1a2 2 0 0 1-2 2 1 1 0 0 0-1 1v2a1 1 0 0 0 1 1 6 6 0 0 0 6-6V5a2 2 0 0 0-2-2z","key":"1ymkrd"}]],"className":"lucide-quote absolute -left-8 -top-8 h-16 w-16 text-gold/10 pointer-events-none"}],["$","h2",null,{"className":"font-serif font-bold text-3xl text-navy mb-6","children":"Biography"}],["$","div",null,{"className":"text-navy/80 text-xl leading-relaxed prose prose-navy max-w-none  prose-headings:font-serif prose-headings:font-bold prose-headings:text-navy  prose-h3:text-3xl prose-h3:mt-10 prose-h3:mb-4 prose-a:text-gold hover:prose-a:text-navy prose-a:transition-colors prose-img:rounded-md prose-img:shadow-md prose-img:mx-auto prose-img:border prose-img:border-gold/20 prose-blockquote:border-l-4 prose-blockquote:border-gold prose-blockquote:pl-8  prose-blockquote:italic prose-blockquote:text-navy/80 prose-blockquote:font-serif prose-blockquote:text-2xl prose-blockquote:ml-8 prose-blockquote:my-10 [&_blockquote_p::before]:hidden [&_blockquote_p::after]:hidden","children":[["$","p","p-0",{"children":"Leonard \"Tim\" Hector (November 24, 1942 – November 12, 2002) was a towering intellectual, a fearless journalist, a radical political activist, and a profound voice for post-colonial liberation in Antigua and the wider Caribbean. Known for his piercing intellect, his relentless opposition to corruption, and his deep-seated commitment to Pan-Africanism and democratic socialism, Hector was a central figure in the Caribbean New Left. For over three decades, he served as the conscience of his nation, wielding his pen as a weapon against the entrenched political dynasties of his era, and fighting tirelessly for the empowerment of the working class."}],"\n",["$","h3","h3-0",{"children":"Early Life and the Seeds of Radicalism"}],"\n",["$","p","p-1",{"children":"Born in St. John’s, Antigua, in 1942, he was named Leonard Hector, but was affectionately nicknamed \"Tim\" by his grandfather—a tribute to the Soviet military commander Marshal Semyon Timoshenko, reflecting the global political awareness that permeated his early environment. Raised primarily by his strong-willed single mother, Mabel Hector, Tim grew up in a working-class household that deeply valued education, debate, and community solidarity."}],"\n",["$","p","p-2",{"children":["Antigua during Hector’s youth was a British colony strictly divided along lines of race and class, dominated by the sugar plantocracy and the emerging political machine of ",["$","$Lb","a-0",{"slug":"v-c-bird","href":"/profiles/v-c-bird","children":"V. C. Bird"}],". Despite the socio-economic barriers, Hector was an exceptionally bright student. He attended the prestigious Antigua Grammar School, where he distinguished himself not only in academics but also in sports, developing a lifelong passion for cricket—a sport he would later analyze through a deeply political and anti-colonial lens."]}],"\n","$Lc","\n","$Ld","\n","$Le","\n","$Lf","\n","$L10","\n","$L11","\n","$L12","\n","$L13","\n","$L14","\n","$L15","\n","$L16","\n","$L17","\n","$L18","\n","$L19","\n","$L1a","\n","$L1b"]}]]}],"$L1c","$L1d",false]}],"$L1e"]}]

a:["$","$L1f",null,{"children":["$","$20",null,{"name":"Next.MetadataOutlet","children":"$@21"}]}]
c:["$","p","p-3",{"children":["His thirst for knowledge led him abroad to Canada, where he pursued higher education at Acadia University and later McGill University. It was during his time in North America in the 1960s that Hector was exposed to the surging currents of the global Civil Rights Movement, the anti-Vietnam War protests, and the emerging Black Power movement. Most crucially, he became a protégé of the legendary Trinidadian Marxist scholar ",["$","$Lb","a-0",{"slug":"c-l-r-james","href":"/profiles/c-l-r-james","children":"C. L. R. James"}],". James’s philosophy—which blended classical Marxism with Pan-Africanism, cultural critique, and a profound faith in the capacity of ordinary people to govern themselves—became the bedrock of Hector’s worldview."]}]
d:["$","blockquote","blockquote-0",{"children":["\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":"\"A society that cannot tolerate radical critique is a society terrified of its own reflection. The duty of the intellectual is not to comfort the powerful, but to endlessly agitate for the powerless.\""}],"\n"]}]
e:["$","h3","h3-1",{"children":"The Return Home and the Formation of the ACLM"}]
f:["$","p","p-4",{"children":"Hector returned to Antigua in 1967, a period of intense political transition as the island moved toward associated statehood. Armed with radical theories and a burning desire for social justice, he quickly clashed with the conservative, paternalistic establishment. He initially threw his support behind the Progressive Labour Movement (PLM) and the Antigua Workers Union, seeking to challenge the dominance of the Bird administration."}]
10:["$","p","p-5",{"children":["However, finding traditional party politics too compromising and insufficiently revolutionary, Hector co-founded the Antigua Caribbean Liberation Movement (ACLM) in the late 1960s. The ACLM was not merely a political party; it was an intellectual vanguard and a mass movement rolled into one. It advocated for true economic independence, the nationalization of key industries, Caribbean integration, and the dismantling of neo-colonial structures. Hector envisioned a Caribbean united not just by trade, but by a shared cultural and political destiny, drawing inspiration from regional leaders like ",["$","$Lb","a-0",{"slug":"maurice-bishop","href":"/profiles/maurice-bishop","children":"Maurice Bishop"}]," of Grenada and ",["$","$Lb","a-1",{"slug":"walter-rodney","href":"/profiles/walter-rodney","children":"Walter Rodney"}]," of Guyana."]}]
11:["$","h3","h3-2",{"children":[["$","em","em-0",{"children":"Outlet"}]," and \"Fan the Flame\""]}]
12:["$","p","p-6",{"children":["Hector’s most enduring and powerful legacy was forged in the pages of ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"Outlet"}],", the newspaper he co-founded in 1968. For over thirty years, ",["$","em","em-1",{"children":"Outlet"}]," served as the premier voice of opposition and radical thought in Antigua. It was read voraciously by citizens across all classes, eagerly anticipated every week for its fearless investigative journalism and scathing political commentary."]}]
13:["$","p","p-7",{"children":["At the heart of ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"Outlet"}]," was Hector’s legendary column, \"Fan the Flame.\" In this column, Hector showcased his brilliance as a \"Renaissance man.\" He wrote with eloquence and fury on an astonishing range of topics: exposing government corruption, analyzing the intricacies of international geopolitics, critiquing Caribbean literature, and writing masterful essays on West Indies cricket. He viewed cricket not just as a game, but as a crucial arena of anti-colonial struggle and cultural self-expression for the Caribbean people."]}]
14:["$","p","p-8",{"children":["Through ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"Outlet"}],", Hector became the primary antagonist to the political dynasty of ",["$","$Lb","a-0",{"slug":"v-c-bird","href":"/profiles/v-c-bird","children":"V. C. Bird"}]," and later his son, ",["$","$Lb","a-1",{"slug":"lester-bird","href":"/profiles/lester-bird","children":"Lester Bird"}],". Hector fiercely criticized their administrations for alleged corruption, nepotism, and the selling out of Antiguan sovereignty to foreign corporate interests. His journalism was dangerous work; he faced constant harassment, libel suits, arrests, and the offices of ",["$","em","em-1",{"children":"Outlet"}]," were targeted and even burned down. Yet, Hector remained unbowed, refusing to be silenced by the state apparatus."]}]
15:["$","blockquote","blockquote-1",{"children":["\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":"\"Tim Hector was the undisputed voice of the Caribbean conscience—a man who wielded history, literature, and political theory as instruments to dismantle the lingering architectures of colonialism.\""}],"\n"]}]
16:["$","h3","h3-3",{"children":"Intellectual Contributions and Regional Impact"}]
17:["$","p","p-9",{"children":"Beyond his local activism, Hector was a highly respected intellectual across the Caribbean and the diaspora. He traveled extensively, lecturing at universities and participating in international conferences. He was a champion of regional integration, arguing that the micro-states of the Caribbean could only survive the pressures of globalization by uniting politically and economically. His alliances with other revolutionary leaders across the region made him a key node in the network of the Caribbean New Left."}]
18:["$","p","p-10",{"children":"Despite never winning mass electoral power—the ACLM’s radical platform often struggled against the deeply entrenched patronage networks of the dominant parties—Hector’s influence was profound. He fundamentally shifted the political discourse in Antigua, forcing accountability, educating the masses on their civil rights, and instilling a sense of pride in Afro-Caribbean identity."}]
19:["$","h3","h3-4",{"children":"Legacy"}]
1a:["$","p","p-11",{"children":"Tim Hector passed away on November 12, 2002, following complications from heart surgery. His death was mourned not just in Antigua, but across the entire Caribbean and the intellectual world."}]
1b:["$","p","p-12",{"children":["He is remembered today not merely as an opposition politician, but as a visionary, a master essayist, and a tireless defender of the poor. The biography ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"Tim Hector: A Caribbean Radical's Story"}]," by Paul Buhle immortalized his contributions, ensuring that his philosophical and political insights would survive for future generations. In the history of the modern Caribbean, Tim Hector remains a brilliant, burning flame—a symbol of the relentless pursuit of freedom, justice, and intellectual integrity."]}]
